objective.statement: Transpose a melody an octave up or down, into the treble or the bass clef.
successCriteria: I know transposing at the octave moves every note eight steps.
I know changing the clef is not enough: the note must also move an octave.
I keep the key signature and write every note in the right place.

explanation.text: To transpose music is to write it higher or lower, so that it sounds higher or lower. In Grade 3 you transpose at the octave, and you may also change from the treble clef to the bass clef, or the other way round. Take middle C. In the treble clef it is on the first ledger line below the stave. The same pitch in the bass clef is on the first ledger line above the stave, as in the picture below.

music.textAlternative: Middle C in the bass clef, on the first ledger line above the stave.

explanation.caption: The same pitch as the treble clef's middle C: this is NOT an octave lower.

music.textAlternative: The C an octave below middle C, in the bass clef, in the second space.

explanation.caption: An octave lower, in the bass clef: the second space.

explanation.text: The last picture is the answer to “write this note an octave lower in the bass clef”. Two things have changed: the clef, and the octave. Writing the same pitch in the new clef would only change the picture, not the sound. To transpose a melody: choose the new clef and the direction. Move every note by one octave, which is eight letter names counting both ends: seven steps of line and space. Keep the key signature, and write any accidentals the notes need. Then check the first and last notes. Moving a note an octave means eight letter names, seven steps of line and space. If the clef changes as well, write the note in its new place: the same pitch in a new clef is not an octave move.

explanation.caption: A melody in the treble clef, in G major.

music.textAlternative: The same melody an octave lower, written in the bass clef, key signature of one sharp.

music.textAlternative: Three notes in the bass clef, C, D and E, an octave below the same notes in the treble clef starting at middle C.

steps: Find the first treble-clef note, middle C, on the first ledger line below the stave.
Move it down one octave: the C in the second space of the bass clef.
Move the other notes the same way, keeping the key signature.
demonstration.textAlternative: C, D and E in the bass clef, an octave lower than the treble-clef notes starting at middle C.

mistakes.wrong-octave: Check the octave: the new version should be exactly one octave higher or lower — not the same pitch, and not two octaves away.
mistakes.wrong-clef: Look at which clef the question asks for — alto and tenor clefs are easy to mix up.
mistakes.wrong-interval: Check the interval given in the question, and count letter names as well as semitones.
mistakes.wrong-direction: Think about the instrument: a B♭ instrument sounds lower than written, so written notes are higher than concert pitch.
mistakes.key-signature-missing: Work out the new key first and write its key signature.
mistakes.accidental-not-adjusted: Accidentals change too. Work out what each altered note is in the original key, then find the same degree in the new key.
mistakes.enharmonic-respelling: That sounds right, but the spelling is wrong. Keep each note the same interval number above its original.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Transpose the key first, then each note, then check accidentals.
